feed.title: A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean

entry.title: A STARK proof of Bitcoin's UTXO set at block 972,500, with circuits proven in Lean
entry.summary:
Header validation involves proof of work, median time checks, and block version signaling. These components are lightweight and can be efficiently validated by light clients without the need for zero-knowledge proofs, as block headers are intrinsically compact and valuable for network security and consensus.
Commitments to per-block undo data, alongside updates to the UTXO set, present a more robust framework for block validation. This approach assumes prior knowledge of block headers and an initial UTXO set commitment, denoted as X, established immediately before the sequence of blocks under consideration. Each block in the sequence, B1 through Bn, is associated with an individual undo data commitment (U1 to Un). For every block Bi, the process ensures that Ui is a subset of the UTXO set preceding Bi and comprises a specifically ordered set of transactions, beginning with the coinbase transaction, which does not spend any UTXOs.
The validation criteria dictate that each UTXO within Ui is spent exactly once by a corresponding transaction. Additional transaction rules include the requirement that coinbase outputs do not exceed the sum of allowed subsidy and total transaction fees, proper handling of signatures, adherence to script logic, enforcement of timelocks and coinbase maturity, and compliance with block weight and signature operation limits. These elements collectively ensure the integrity and consistency of the evolving UTXO set.
A proof system centered on validating UTXO set updates is likely to offer greater longevity and adaptability compared to per-block validation mechanisms. Per-block validation tends to be more susceptible to changes introduced by soft forks, whereas focusing on UTXO set verification addresses the core challenge of confirming new blocks without reprocessing the entire history. By equipping the validation system with only the block and its corresponding undo data or commitment, rather than the full UTXO set, there is potential to achieve more efficient proof constructions.
Additionally, maintaining commitments to undo data could benefit protocols like swiftsync, where direct execution of validation code remains necessary. Generalizing the specification of UTXO set maintenance to accommodate both valid and invalid blocks would further enhance the robustness and clarity of the protocol.
